p.s: Most denied health insurance claims are never appealed.

Not because the denial was right — often it isn't — but because figuring out whether a denial reason is even legitimate, and drafting a correctly-argued appeal inside a strict filing window, is a specialized, exhausting task nobody has the bandwidth for while sick, injured, or already stressed about a bill.
A lot of those denials are pure mechanical billing errors — an outdated diagnosis code, a typo — that would be reprocessed immediately if someone just caught it and said so.

This is ClaimClarity — an agent built with the Strands Agents SDK that reads your denial notice, checks it against real ICD-10 coding rules and your plan's own terms, and drafts the appeal — or tells you honestly when it's not worth fighting.
ClaimClarity is built for the people staring down an Explanation of Benefits with no billing background:
patients managing their own care, family caregivers handling a parent's bills, and the small clinics and billing offices too short-staffed to chase every denial by hand.

What used to mean hours of confusion, or just paying a bill you didn't actually owe, now runs unattended — and because it never recommends fighting a denial that's genuinely valid, you're not wasting your appeal window on a fight you can't win either.
Let's watch it work on a real example: a denial notice with two line items on it, both billed under the same diagnosis code.

One click, and an orchestrator agent takes over. Watch the activity log — this is a real tool call happening live, not a canned animation: instead of reasoning about medical coding from a language model's memory, which is a common source of confidently wrong billing advice, the Denial Investigator actually calls a real ICD-10 lookup tool before concluding anything about a code.

On this run, it caught that one line item's diagnosis code was retired for billing purposes back in twenty twenty-two — a mechanical billing error — and found the correct, specific replacement code. The second line item, a massage therapy charge, it correctly classified as a valid denial: a genuine plan exclusion, no amount of coding fixes it. Two identically-worded denials, told apart correctly.

A second, independent investigation runs right after — same claim, same real coding tools, but no knowledge of the first investigator's conclusion. Because every finding carries a stable procedure code, comparing the two doesn't even need another model call: it's a plain code diff, and any disagreement forces that line item to needs review instead of trusting either investigation alone.

Then the Appeal Drafter writes a real, ready-to-send appeal letter for the item worth appealing, and an honest plain-language explanation for the one that isn't — instead of drafting a doomed letter just to be agreeable.

Nothing gets sent automatically. The run lands in an approval panel — because whoever's reading this is often not watching every file get written; they're sick, or stressed, or just busy — and a human has to actually approve it, edits included, before it's marked done.
And everything funnels into exactly one place a stressed patient actually needs to read: Decisions Needed.
What's worth appealing, what isn't and why, and the deadline.
ClaimClarity drafts. It doesn't submit — a human always reviews and sends the appeal, which is the entire point of that approval panel.

And the same run also watches for a pattern: if the same insurer denies the same thing more than once across a patient's history, that gets surfaced too — a materially stronger fact for an appeal than one denial looked at alone.
Next, genuinely: a full, live ICD-10-CM data source instead of a curated demo subset, and support for more insurers' plan formats.
ClaimClarity — built with the Strands Agents SDK, for the Agents for Humans Hackathon. Read the denial once. Know what's actually worth fighting.
